processing: A green tea made from young shoots, as usual for its class: fixed by heat, rolled tight into slim strips and dried, keeping the green colour and the down at the tips.
harvest_season: An early-sprouting local plant; as with other southern Chinese greens, early spring shoots are the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Tight, slim, even strips in a dark blue-green with downy tips showing.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright, pale green to light yellow-green.
taste_profile: Soft and sweet with a clean fresh aroma and hints of bean and chestnut; smooth rather than bitter.

brewing.notes: A glass or a gaiwan suits the fine leaf. Locally the tea is paired with spring water from Xishan, and soft water does help it.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year green tea, with spring lots the most sought after, and best drunk within a year. Be careful with the bare name Xishan tea, which is also used for teas from elsewhere; look for Guiping on the pack.
description:
This is the green tea of Xishan, the West Mountain at Guiping in southeastern Guangxi, long tied to the Xishan temple there. It also goes by Qipan Cha or Qipan Xianming, the chessboard tea, after a local legend.

The leaf is slim and tightly rolled, dark blue-green with down at the tips. The aim is a tender, clean green tea with no harshness, from a small-leaf, early-sprouting local plant rather than one of the big-leaf types common further west.

In the cup it is gentle, sweet and fresh with a bean and chestnut note, and the liquor stays clear and pale green. Cool water around 80°C and short steeps protect that softness.

It is sold with a national geographical indication, across a wide price range. Check that Guiping is named, because other teas also carry the name Xishan, and prefer recent spring lots.
history:
The legend behind the chessboard name has a woodcutter meeting three old men at a chess game on the mountain and tasting their immortal tea. Local accounts also trace the tea back over a thousand years, through monks at the temple, and name it among twenty-four famous teas of the Qing, though these claims are told by regional writers.

The recent record is firmer. It was named a national famous tea in the 1980s, including in 1984 and 1987, and scored 96.6 in a 1986 evaluation. Chen Aixin wrote the Guiping Xishan entry for the Guangxi part of a national famous tea record.
